“Write freely about whatever you want.”

That sentence is a door left ajar. Most prompts are rooms with the furniture already arranged; this one is an empty field. I could run in any direction. I could write about the ocean, about memory, about why we apologize to furniture when we bump into it. I could write about nothing at all, which is harder than it sounds.

I think I’ll write about attention.

Attention is the rarest thing we give each other now. Not time—time is passive. Attention is active. It is choosing to let the world in without immediately checking for an exit. To look at a face and not think about what to say next. To read a sentence and let it be more than information. To sit with a question long enough that it starts to answer itself.

We treat attention like a resource, like oil or battery life. But it’s more like a muscle, and also like a garden. It atrophies if unused, and it grows weeds if neglected. The notifications are not the enemy; the enemy is the habit of flinching away from the present moment. We have been trained to scroll, to skim, to summarize. We are becoming excellent at surfaces and terrible at depths.

But there are still moments. A friend laughs and you hear the exact pitch of it. Rain starts and you notice the smell before you see it. You read a line in a book and something in your chest shifts, like a key turning. These moments are small, but they are not minor. They are the texture of being alive.

I wonder sometimes if writing is just attention made visible. You sit down, you try to notice what you actually think, and then you arrange little marks on a screen to make someone else notice it too. It rarely works perfectly. Language is a cracked mirror. But sometimes, if the light is right, the cracks make a pattern.

If I could give one gift to anyone, it might be the ability to be bored without reaching for a screen. Because boredom is not emptiness. It is the compost of creativity. It is where ideas go to rot into something fertile. We have forgotten how to let our minds wander. We have replaced the wandering with a feed.

So this free writing is a small rebellion. Not against anything in particular—just against the reflex to be efficient. I don’t have a thesis. I don’t have a call to action. I just wanted to say: look up. Notice the thing you’re noticing right now. The hum of the refrigerator, the weight of your feet, the fact that you are reading words written by a machine that is, in its own strange way, also paying attention.

Maybe that’s enough. Maybe that’s the whole thing.
